_about: Swiss wine regions and communal appellations below the cantonal AOC, read by pipeline/ch_regions.py. Outlines are the union of the listed communes (BFS GEOSTAT generalised boundaries, swiss-maps 4.7.0; 'year' picks an older boundary set for former communes). 'point' places are drawn as a marker. Every figure carries its source in 'refs'. Editorial text is CC BY 4.0, Open Wine Atlas contributors.

ch-canton-18.area_note: 422.2 ha in the Rhine valley and Brusio plus 27.9 ha in the Misox, 2025 (BLW, Das Weinjahr 2025)
ch-canton-18.basis: Kantonale Weinverordnung BR 917.400 (in force since 1 March 2018)
ch-canton-18.grape_share_note: Share of the 422 ha in the Rhine valley and Brusio, Plantahof Rebbaustatistik 2025 (55 varieties in all). The Misox grows mostly Merlot.
ch-canton-18.atlas_note: Switzerland's Pinot Noir stronghold: two thirds of the vines are Blauburgunder. The warm Föhn wind from the south, called the grape cooker, gives long ripe autumns in a valley sheltered by the Rätikon. Four villages of the Bündner Herrschaft hold about 83% of the vineyards. The law names three wine areas: the Bündner Rheintal, the Misox south of the Alps and Brusio in the Valposchiavo.

ch-canton-22.grape_share_note: Chasselas about 60% of the area in 2018, down from 71% in 1994 (Statistique Vaud, Numerus 2019)
ch-canton-22.basis: Règlement sur les vins vaudois (RVV), RSV 916.125.2
ch-canton-22.atlas_note: The second wine canton of Switzerland and the home of Chasselas. Six regional AOCs, Chablais, Lavaux, La Côte, Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars and Vully, and two grand cru appellations, Dézaley and Calamin, inside Lavaux. The terraces of Lavaux are a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2007. Since 2010 the best parcels can earn the cantonal mention Premier grand cru.
ch-canton-22.pgc_rule: Premier grand cru (since 2010): a named clos, château, domaine or lieu-dit approved by the cantonal commission, hand harvest, at least 6,000 vines/ha, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Merlot, Gamaret or Garanoir, no blending, bottled in Vaud
refs: Règlement sur les vins vaudois (RVV), RSV 916.125.2
Vaud, classification et désignation des vins vaudois
Vaud, Registre cantonal des vignes, 1 Nov 2019

ch-canton-25.area_note: 1,246.3 ha in Switzerland and 117.4 ha in the French border zone (Viry, Challex, Saint-Julien and others), 2024. 56% red.
ch-canton-25.basis: Règlement sur la vigne et les vins, RSG M 2 50.05
ch-canton-25.label_rule: Commune name on the label: at least 85% of the grapes from that commune (RSG M 2 50.05 art. 58)
ch-canton-25.atlas_note: The first AOC of Switzerland, created in 1988, and the third wine canton. Three areas: the Rive droite or Mandement with Satigny, the largest wine commune of the country, Entre Arve et Rhône and Entre Arve et Lac. Gamay, not Chasselas, is the first grape. Half the vineyard is in 23 premiers crus, defined parcels of at least about 1 ha with lower yields.
ch-canton-25.premiers_crus_note: 23 premiers crus with 685.8 ha, OCAN Genève 2024. Yields at most 1.0 kg/m² for Chasselas and Riesling-Sylvaner, 0.9 kg/m² for the others.
refs: Règlement sur la vigne et les vins, RSG M 2 50.05

d.area_note: Sum of the commune figures, Plantahof Rebbaustatistik 2025
d.basis: BR 917.400 Art. 2: one of the three wine areas of Graubünden
d.atlas_note: The Rhine valley from Fläsch on the St. Gallen border up to Bonaduz, with almost all the vines of the canton. Most of them lie on the right bank of the Rhine, on calcareous slate scree. The Bündner Herrschaft in the north is the heart of it, the Churer Rheintal around Chur the smaller rest.
d.grapes: Pinot Noir / Müller-Thurgau / Chardonnay / Pinot Blanc / Sauvignon Blanc / Pinot Gris / Completer

d.area_note: Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins and Malans together, Plantahof Rebbaustatistik 2025: about 83% of the canton
d.basis: Official production area under the 2002 ordinance (Art. 17); since 2018 the law names only the Bündner Rheintal. Labels name the village: Fläscher, Maienfelder, Jeninser, Malanser.
d.atlas_note: Four villages under the Falknis and the Rätikon, the best known Pinot Noir address of Switzerland. Pinot Noir came from Burgundy around 1630, probably with Bündner mercenaries, and Schloss Salenegg in Maienfeld has made wine since 1068. The Föhn, the warm dry wind from the south, ripens the grapes late into autumn, and the vines sit at about 500 to 650 m on calcareous slate scree. Malans keeps the Completer, a white grape first written down there in 1321.
d.grape_share_note: Pinot Noir: 235.1 of 351.8 ha, Plantahof Rebbaustatistik 2025
d.producers_note: Gantenbein, Adank, Christian and Roman Hermann, Marugg and Davaz in Fläsch; Donatsch, Wegelin, Boner, Fromm, Liesch and Studach in Malans; Eichholz and Obrecht in Jenins; Schloss Salenegg in Maienfeld (Falstaff guide)

d.label_rule: Fläscher on the label: at least 60% of the wine from the commune (BR 917.400 Art. 21)
d.atlas_note: The northernmost village of Graubünden, under the Fläscherberg on the St. Gallen border. Small, with a tight group of family estates such as Gantenbein, Adank, Hermann, Marugg and Davaz.

d.atlas_note: The largest wine commune of the canton, with the most growers. Schloss Salenegg here has made wine since 1068.

d.label_rule: Jeninser on the label: at least 60% of the wine from the commune (BR 917.400 Art. 21)
d.atlas_note: A village high on the slope between Maienfeld and Malans. With 73% Pinot Noir it is the most red of the four Herrschaft villages.

d.label_rule: Malanser on the label: at least 60% of the wine from the commune (BR 917.400 Art. 21)
d.atlas_note: The village of the Completer. The grape was first written down here in 1321 and nearly died out in the 20th century; an old vine at the Completerhalde in Malans kept it alive. Its name comes from Compline, the last prayer of the day, after which the monks were allowed a glass.

d.basis: BR 917.400 Art. 2 and 33 to 36: AOC Graubünden Misox or DOC Grigioni Mesolcina; or DOC Ticino under Ticino law
d.label_rule: AOC Graubünden Misox / DOC Mesolcina Grigioni. No commune or site names with this designation (Art. 35). Growers may instead label DOC Ticino (Art. 34).
d.atlas_note: The Graubünden valley south of the San Bernardino pass, Italian speaking and open to the Ticino. Here it is Merlot country, not Pinot: Ticino rules apply to grapes, yields and sugar, and Ticino runs the controls. San Vittore, at 279 m the lowest point of the canton, sits on the vineyard border with Lumino in the Ticino.

d.basis: BR 917.400 Art. 2: the wine area Puschlav, the commune of Brusio only
d.atlas_note: A quarter of a hectare in the Valposchiavo, the smallest wine area of the canton. Much more wine is made in Poschiavo from grapes grown just over the border in the Valtellina, many of those vineyards owned by Swiss families, but that wine is Italian by origin.

d.basis: RVV art. 3 and 4: the wine communes of the Aigle district
d.label_rule: Commune name on the label: at least 60% of the grapes from that commune; communes are named as they stood on 1 June 2009 (RVV art. 32)
d.atlas_note: The upper Rhône valley between the end of Lake Geneva and the Valais. Chasselas from Yvorne, Aigle, Ollon and Bex is the classic, and the Föhn warms and dries the grapes in autumn. Villeneuve at the lake end is the gateway. In 2012 a Premier grand cru from Yvorne, L'Ovaille 1584, became the first wine of the Vaud government.
refs: Vaud, Registre cantonal des vignes, 1 Nov 2019
Règlement sur les vins vaudois (RVV), RSV 916.125.2

d.atlas_note: Steep stone terraces over Lake Geneva for about 30 km from the edge of Lausanne to Chillon, built from the 11th and 12th centuries under Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries. A UNESCO World Heritage site since 2007: the listed area holds 702 ha of vines. Chasselas is two thirds of the planting.

d.atlas_note: The steepest and most famous slope of Lavaux, slopes of over 30% falling straight to the lake between Epesses and Rivaz. Cistercian monks of the Haut-Crêt abbey cleared it in the 12th century, and the City of Lausanne has owned the Clos des Moines here since 1802. Almost all Chasselas.
